title: Phillips County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Phillips County wells have a 270 ft median depth. See reported yields, water-level trends and finished-well costs of about $15,400-$26,800.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Phillips County
intro_html:
A Phillips County well budget needs to account for more than drilling depth. Reported wells have a median depth of 270 ft, but the historical water-level records also point toward deeper water over time. That matters when evaluating an existing well or choosing a location for a new one.

Colorado DWR records include 2,812 permitted wells countywide, with 988 recorded as constructed. These figures cover different well uses, not just homes. For property around Holyoke, Haxtun, Amherst or Paoli, county averages are a starting point; nearby construction logs and the property's actual permit deserve more weight.

sections.heading: Around Holyoke and Haxtun, Budget for More Than a Shallow Well
sections.html:
Among the 1,480 wells reporting depth, the median is 270 ft and the middle half runs 218-305 ft. That is a useful range for comparing preliminary bids, not a promise that drilling will stop there. The 90th-percentile depth is 340 ft, and the deepest recorded well reaches 515 ft. Ask how a bid handles additional footage and casing.

Phillips County's drilling ground is alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. Permits name the Ogallala for 1,087 wells and the High Plains Aquifer for 22. Another 1,682 fall under an unnamed / fractured-bedrock label; that broad records category should not be read as proof of granite beneath your lot. Local sediment layers and the water-bearing interval determine the actual completion.

sections.heading: A 20 gpm Median Does Not Describe Every Phillips County Well
sections.html:
The 505 reported pump yields have a median of 20.0 gpm, with the middle half spanning 14.0-600.0 gpm. That wide spread needs context: irrigation appears on 47% of permits, domestic/household use on 34%, and stock use on 28%. This is not a household-only yield sample, and a high-capacity irrigation well is a poor direct comparison for a home well.

Reported yields include 2% at 1-5 gpm and 0% under 1 gpm. Those records do not establish that every attempted well succeeded. For a purchase, get a current pumping and recovery test rather than relying on the original reported yield. The result should be evaluated against household demand and the uses allowed by the permit.

sections.heading: Phillips County's Water-Level Records Point Deeper
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the bottom of the well. Across 172 reports, the median is 158 ft below ground, with the middle half at 121-195 ft. A well's total depth alone does not tell you how much usable water remains above its pump.

The decade medians deepen from 121 ft in the 1960s to 134 ft in the 1970s, 182 ft in the 2010s and 190 ft in the 2020s. That pattern is consistent with a declining water table. It is not a measured decline at every property: the medians may represent different wells and locations. Before buying, compare the well's current static and pumping levels with its construction log and earlier measurements.

sections.heading: A Long Drilling Record, With Permits Through 2025
sections.html:
Phillips County's permit history includes 33 permits in the 1950s and 377 in the 1970s. Later records show 333 in the 1990s, 278 in the 2000s, 182 in the 2010s and 111 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. The latest decade is incomplete, so its count should not be treated as a finished comparison.

The most active listed drillers are Wellstone Industries Dba Twiss & Wilson Drilling Inc (Twiss, Raymond L.), with 345 records; Stewart Drilling Co. (Stewart, Dennis W.), with 105; and Jim Feighny & Sons (Feighny, Jim), with 100. These are historical record counts, not confirmation of current availability. Permit issuance also does not establish that a well was constructed.

sections.heading: Plan on a Finished-Well Budget, Not Just Footage
sections.html:
The Phillips County cost model uses $35-$55 per foot for drilling in alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 270 ft median depth, the drilled hole is about $9,400-$14,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $15,400-$26,800.

Use that finished range as an early planning allowance, then get a site-specific written bid. Confirm the proposed depth, casing and grout, pump selection, trench route and electrical scope. Ask how testing and unexpected drilling conditions are priced. A property needing a deeper completion or a different equipment layout will not necessarily fit the median-depth model. Keep driveway, septic and home construction costs separate from the well allowance.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Well Condition Before Closing
sections.html:
The environmental mapping identifies 14 PFAS sampling/contamination sites within about 10 miles. That is a screening flag, not proof that a particular well contains PFAS. The same mapping lists 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites, but those counts do not establish drinking-water safety.

Have a qualified laboratory test the property's water for bacteria and nitrate, and discuss PFAS testing in light of nearby site information. Inspect the wellhead, casing and surface drainage for routes that could admit contamination. Reported yield data cannot tell you the chance of a dry hole on an unbuilt lot. For an existing home, pair water testing with a pumping test; for construction, coordinate the well location with septic setbacks, building placement and service access.

sections.heading: For a Phillips County Lot, Start With the Permit and Nearby Logs
sections.html:
Before committing to land near Amherst, Paoli, Holyoke or Haxtun, compare neighboring well depths, aquifer descriptions and recent water-level measurements. Countywide numbers are more useful than distant assumptions, but the closest comparable wells usually provide a better basis for a drilling conversation. Records across the boundary in Sedgwick County or Yuma County may help when the geology is comparable.

Have DWR confirm the property's permitting path and allowed uses. Do not assume a household well authorizes livestock, lawn watering or irrigation. Exempt permits carry specific conditions, and some nonexempt uses may require augmentation. Make the purchase decision around a workable plan for water supply, septic, building placement and drilling access—not simply the presence of a permit on a map.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Phillips County, Colorado?
faq.a: Reported wells have a median depth of 270 ft, and the middle half falls between 218 and 305 ft. The 90th-percentile depth is 340 ft. Those figures come from 1,480 depth reports across different well uses. For a specific lot, nearby logs and the intended water-bearing interval are better bid inputs than the county median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Phillips County?
faq.a: The local model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 270 ft median depth, the drilled hole is about $9,400-$14,800, while a finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $15,400-$26,800. Treat these as planning figures, then request a written bid that identifies casing, equipment, testing and additional-footage charges.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Phillips County?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 20.0 gpm, with the middle half ranging from 14.0 to 600.0 gpm. Irrigation appears on 47% of permits, so these are not strictly household-well results. A current pumping and recovery test is the best way to assess an existing well against your intended demand and permitted uses.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Phillips County?
faq.a: County records cannot establish whether a particular well is safe. Mapping shows 14 PFAS sampling/contamination sites within about 10 miles, which warrants checking local site information but does not prove contamination at your property. Test the actual well water for bacteria and nitrate, discuss PFAS testing with a qualified laboratory, and inspect the wellhead and casing.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Phillips County?
faq.a: The available decade medians suggest deeper water over time: 121 ft below ground in the 1960s, 134 ft in the 1970s, 182 ft in the 2010s and 190 ft in the 2020s. These are not repeated measurements of every well. Check current static and pumping levels at the property before drawing conclusions about its remaining water supply.
